passage: On the playground in Manchester, two older boys flicked paper balls at Tariq and called him names. Tariq hunched his shoulders, ducked his head and covered his face with both arms. The boys laughed. Rosa, eating her apple on the bench, watched. The way he curled up didn't look weak or funny to her. It looked frightened, and hurt. She stood up. “Stop it,” she said, loud and steady. The boys shrugged and wandered off. Rosa walked to Tariq. “Come with me,” she said. “Let's tell Ms Hayes.” Tariq lowered his arms and nodded.

qa.q: What did the older boys flick at Tariq?
qa.a: They flicked paper balls at him.

qa.q: What did Rosa read in Tariq's ducked head and covered face, and how sure can she be?
qa.a: She read fear and hurt, not weakness. She cannot be completely sure, but the hunched shoulders and covered face fit that reading.

qa.q: What did Rosa do that was a wise response?
qa.a: She told the boys to stop, went to Tariq and took him to tell a teacher, instead of ignoring it or joining in.

qa.q: How might Tariq feel when Rosa steps in?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone, since he lowered his arms and nodded. He may still feel shaky or embarrassed.

grounding: A child recognises that a peer recoiling from a taunt is frightened or hurt, stops it and tells a teacher.

passage: In the hostel dining hall, three older boys at the next table started mocking Anand's haircut, calling out, “Bald eagle!” Anand shrank into his chair, pulled his shoulders up and covered his face with his hands. Tarun, who was standing in the queue with his plate, saw it. He thought about laughing along, like the others, but Anand's hands were shaking. Tarun put his plate down. “That's enough, leave him alone,” he said. Then he sat beside Anand. “Let's tell the warden.” Anand lowered his hands, eyes red. “Okay.”

qa.q: What did the boys call out at Anand?
qa.a: They called out, “Bald eagle!”

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when he shrank into his chair and covered his face, and what else might it be?
qa.a: Probably fear and hurt, since his hands were shaking, which is why Tarun stopped and acted. It could also have been embarrassment about the taunt over his haircut.

qa.q: What could Tarun and Anand do next after telling the warden?
qa.a: Stay together, let the warden speak with the older boys, and check in with Anand later so he does not feel alone.

qa.q: How might the older boys see what they did?
qa.a: They may think it was harmless teasing, not noticing Anand's fear. Tarun's words may make them realise it was hurting him.

grounding: A child sees a peer shrink and cover the face during a taunt, stops it and tells an adult.

passage: I'm Keerthana. At break, some kids were flicking rubber bands at Sanjay and calling him “Bandar.” Preeti was laughing with them at first. Then Sanjay ducked, arms over his face, and his whole body curled against the wall. Preeti's laugh stopped. She looked at him for a long moment, then stepped in front of him and said, “Stop. He's scared, can't you see?” The others groaned and drifted off. Preeti crouched and asked Sanjay if a band had hit his eye. Then she walked straight to the staff room with him. Ms Rao came out, took Sanjay to the nurse and spoke to the group before the bell.

qa.q: What were the kids calling Sanjay?
qa.a: They were calling him “Bandar.”

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when her laugh stopped?
qa.a: She was probably shocked and uncomfortable, seeing from Sanjay's curled body that he was frightened, not playing along.

qa.q: Which of Preeti's steps were wise?
qa.a: She stopped joining in, told the others to stop, checked if Sanjay was hurt and took him to a teacher straight away.

qa.q: What was the break like for Sanjay?
qa.a: Sanjay was scared and possibly in pain, curling against the wall to protect his face from the rubber bands.

grounding: Shows a child recognising that a peer's ducking and covering the face means fear, then stopping, helping and telling a teacher.

passage: Monday: On the stairs, two older girls mimicked Shreya's accent. Shreya shrank against the railing, shoulders up to her ears. Devika, walking behind, thought, She's just shy, and kept going. Wednesday: The same girls blocked the stairs. One raised her hand fast, as if to slap, and Shreya flinched and covered her face with both arms. The girl laughed. “Scaredy cat.” This time Devika saw the trembling. She stepped beside Shreya. “Leave her alone.” Then she took Shreya's hand and went straight to Mrs Bhatia, who listened, wrote it all down and called both girls to her office that afternoon. Friday: Shreya sat with Devika at lunch.

qa.q: Who did Devika take Shreya to?
qa.a: Devika took Shreya to Mrs Bhatia.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she covered her face?
qa.a: Shreya was frightened, expecting to be hit; her trembling showed fear, not weakness.

qa.q: What did Devika do differently on Wednesday, and why was it right?
qa.a: She stood beside Shreya, told the girls to stop and took her to a teacher straight away, instead of walking past.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had kept walking on Wednesday?
qa.a: Shreya would have faced the girls alone, and the teacher might never have learned about the bullying.

grounding: Shows a child learning to read a peer's shrinking and face-covering as fear, and stepping in, helping and telling a teacher.

passage: Mridul, you asked why I get angry about bullying. Let your Vishal Dadu tell you something I'm not proud of. In Class 5, a big boy named Bhola used to raise his fist at a thin boy, Keshav, just to watch him flinch. Keshav would duck and cover his head with both arms, and everyone laughed, and so did I. I told myself Keshav was weak. One day I saw his arms up and his eyes shut tight, and I understood: he was terrified. I went to our headmaster that same afternoon. He called Bhola in and had Keshav sit near the office at break. I wished I had gone sooner.

qa.q: What did Bhola do to Keshav?
qa.a: Bhola used to raise his fist at Keshav just to watch him flinch.

qa.q: What was Keshav feeling when he ducked and covered his head?
qa.a: Keshav was terrified, not weak, as young Vishal finally saw from his shut eyes and raised arms.

qa.q: What choice did young Vishal make, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He went to the headmaster that same afternoon, which led to Bhola being called in and Keshav being kept safer.

qa.q: How might Keshav have felt about the classmates who laughed?
qa.a: Keshav probably felt alone and humiliated, seeing even the others laugh at his fear.

grounding: Shows a child realising that a peer's ducking during threats means fear, not weakness, and telling an adult the same day.

passage:
Rain hammered the roof of the school bus, and the attendant was up front arguing with the driver about the wipers. At the back, two Class 7 boys leaned over Reena's seat. "Oi, specky! Show us your frog eyes." One flicked her glasses.

Reena ducked, pulled her hood down and covered her face with both arms.

Sabina's friend giggled. "She's such a baby."

Sabina didn't laugh. That wasn't babyish; Reena was shaking. "Stop it," Sabina said loudly, and slid in beside Reena. At the school gate she took Reena straight to Mrs Pinto on duty and told her everything. Mrs Pinto listened, thanked them both and sent for the two boys before first period.

qa.q: What did one of the boys flick?
qa.a: Reena's glasses.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling as she ducked and covered her face?
qa.a: Frightened and hurt by the taunts, not babyish; her shaking shows how scared she was.

qa.q: Which choices did Sabina make that helped Reena?
qa.a: She refused to laugh, told the boys to stop, sat beside Reena and took her straight to Mrs Pinto, a teacher.

qa.q: How did Sabina's friend read Reena's ducking?
qa.a: The friend saw it as babyish and giggled, missing that Reena was frightened and in pain.

grounding: It shows a child recognising a peer's ducking and face-covering during a taunt as fear, stopping, helping and telling a teacher.
